## Goal

Demonstrate the central limit theorem

### Subgoals

- Learn about RMarkdown (the thing you're reading now)
- Refactor some code, think about simplification

### prerequisites for the central limit demonstration

- generator of numbers from some distribution
- give some impression of the distribution
- display the distribution of the means

Let's have a look at how to create some skewed distributions with built-in R functions

```{r distributions}

# The following example was taken from: https://statisticsglobe.com/draw-normal-left-right-skewed-distributions-r

set.seed(35486)                    # Create random distributions
data <- data.frame(x1 = rbeta(1000, 10, 2),
                   x2 = rbeta(1000, 5, 2),
                   x3 = rnorm(1000),
                   x4 = rbeta(1000, 2, 5),
                   x5 = rbeta(1000, 2, 10))

head(data)                         # Print head of data
```

As you can see, we're using the beta distribution, which is defined as

$\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) = \displaystyle \frac{x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}$

where

$\mathrm{B}(\alpha, \beta)=\displaystyle \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha + \beta)}$

and $\Gamma$ is the Gamma function: $\Gamma(z) = \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} t^{z-1} e^{-t}\mathrm dt$

see also <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_distribution>

All of this is not very relevant, but to show how to write maths: <https://rpruim.github.io/s341/S19/from-class/MathinRmd.html>

## Here are some plots to show what the distributions look like graphically

Here I've used 'base R' functions, because we're going to talk about ggplot2 later in this course.

```{r densityplots, echo=FALSE}
plot(density(data$x1), col = 2,    # Overlay all columns as densities
     xlim = c(- 3, 3),
     ylim = c(0, 5))
lines(density(data$x2), col = 3)

lines(density(data$x3), col = 4)
lines(density(data$x4), col = 5)
lines(density(data$x5), col = 6)
legend("topleft",                  # Add legend to plot
       legend = c("x1 = rbeta(1000, 10, 2)",
                  "x2 = rbeta(1000, 5, 2)",
                  "x3 = rnorm(1000)",
                  "x4 = rbeta(1000, 2, 5)",
                  "x5 = rbeta(1000, 2, 10)"),
       col = 2:6,
       lty = 1,
       cex = 0.8)

```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

# Assignment

## Laying the basis: Initial functions

- Create a function to create a list with 300 vectors with 1000 samples each using one of the rbeta distributions (pick your own parameters)
- Create a function to calculate a vector with the averages of all of these vectors
- Create q-q plots. Use this to show the normality of one of the original distributions, and of the resulting averages vector

```{r initial function, eval=FALSE}
# set 'eval=TRUE' (or remove it) for this block to be interpreted by R

generate_dataset <- function() {
  result <- list()
  for (i in 1:300) {
    result[[i]] <- rbeta(1000, 10, 2)
  }
  return(result)
}

calculate_mean_values <- function(dataset) {
  result <- c()
  for (i in 1:300) {
    result <- c(result, mean(dataset[[i]]))
  }
  return(result)
}

random_samples <- generate_dataset()
mean_values <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples)

qqnorm(random_samples[[1]])
qqnorm(mean_values)

#ik heb de mean evt nog op deze manier gedaan (stukje van de code): 

calculate_mean_values <- function(generate_dataset) { 
  avarages<- sapply(generate_dataset, mean) 
  return(avarages)
}

random_samples <- generate_dataset()
mean_values <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples)


```

## Refactoring: adding functionality

We'd like to be able to set the number of datasets, and the number of samples per dataset. Copy the code block from above (not very DRY, but you will have the history of your thought process in this document)

the generate_dataset function should now take some arguments, being n for the number of datasets, and m for the number of samples in each dataset

We're *refactoring*, so make sure that the **generate_dataset()** call still works.

```{r first parameters}
generate_dataset <- function(n = 300, m = 1000) {
  result <- list()
  for (i in 1:n) {
    result[[i]] <- rbeta(m, 10, 2)
  }
  return(result)
}

calculate_mean_values <- function(dataset) {
  result <- c()
  for (i in 1:length(dataset)) {
    result <- c(result, mean(dataset[[i]]))
  }
  return(result)
}

random_samples <- generate_dataset()
mean_values <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples)

qqnorm(random_samples[[1]])
qqnorm(mean_values)

```

## Different alpha and beta arguments

Copy your refactored (working) code again and now add code to vary alpha and beta values for the rbeta function. Again, make sure the argument-less call gives the same results as before.

```{r add alpha and beta parameters}

generate_dataset <- function(n = 300, m = 1000, a = 10, b = 2) {
  result <- list()
  for (i in 1:n) {
    result[[i]] <- rbeta(m,a,b)
  }
  return(result)
}

calculate_mean_values <- function(dataset) {
  result <- c()
  for (i in 1:length(dataset)) {
    result <- c(result, mean(dataset[[i]]))
  }
  return(result)
}

random_samples <- generate_dataset()
mean_values <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples)

qqnorm(random_samples[[1]])
qqnorm(mean_values)

```

## Ambitious exercise

So far we have only used rbeta functions. Now make it possible to choose your function in the **generate_dataset** call

Hints: - You can pass a function as an argument, and call this function by using the argument name in your function - Note that the random number functions all start with the number of samples, and are followed with specific arguments for the required distribution - examples are runif, rnorm, rbeta, look them up with `?` - You can pass *any* number of arguments by using '...' in the argument list. This can be passed on to functions inside your function body

```{r free form random argument}
generate_dataset <- function(n = 300, m = 1000, a = 10, b = 2, func = rbeta) {
  result <- list()
  for (i in 1:n) {
    result[[i]] <- func(m,a,b)
  }
  return(result)
}

calculate_mean_values <- function(dataset) {
  result <- c()
  for (i in 1:length(dataset)) {
    result <- c(result, mean(dataset[[i]]))
  }
  return(result)
}


random_samples <- generate_dataset()
mean_values <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples)

qqnorm(random_samples[[6]])
qqnorm(mean_values, main = "Mean values")

```

## Wrapping it up

Lastly you take the role of the documentation writer. Use your newly gained knowledge about rmarkdown to describe your last function in more detail. It's good / allowed to split your final code block into smaller pieces, and also to demonstrate the use of the different functions. Start with a couple of lines with motivation about your functions, say how the functions work, and show that the Central Limit Theorem works for different distribution types. No need for long discussions, a few sentences each suffices.

**Answer**:\
The functions generated make it easy to form an amount of datasets with random sampling. It makes it easy to call on to later, as you would only need to call the function and, if wanted, specify if the number of datasets, samples, function, or the alpha or beta differs from the given "standard" that is programmed in the function. The functions are easy to work with and easy to call whenever you want to plot or work with them later.

# Demonstrating the Central Limit Theorem

**Answer**:\
With a large enough sample size, the mean of a sample of data will be closer to the mean of the overall population in question as the sample size increases, notwithstanding the actual distribution of the data. The mean will therefore adhere to a normal distribution.
